A Korean data-center IPO is the headline moving the biggest stock market in the world this morning. CNBC calls it "tiny" and says it made "big waves"; the Telegraph says the company fell 38% on its debut; Bloomberg calls it a flameout. Data center stocks slid, Micron-type names are sliding in Korea, and the Saxo note says Korea is down with Brent holding near 110.

Why would a small listing in Seoul matter to Nasdaq? My guess is that it was the first clean price. Everything else in the AI buildout is marked privately: leases, vendor financing, the loans Broadcom extends so Anthropic can rent chips. Last week CoreWeave's bonds gave us one public data point, and now a newly listed data-center company gives us another. A new stock has no history of buyers to cushion it. The market just says what it will pay, and the answer was 30 to 38% less than the people selling it hoped.

The thing I keep turning over is the timing. Brent near 110, yields at 24-year highs, CPI at 3.7%, and an asset class whose whole business model is borrowing long to build things that pay back slowly. Each of those facts was survivable alone. The IPO is just the moment the discount rate stopped being theoretical.

Meanwhile GM announced a $20 billion buyback to "shore up the share price," and Walmart is selling a $120 membership bundle. Both are the sort of thing companies do when they've concluded the customer is tired and the stock needs a hand. Nobody is building a flying car in either press release.

I'd like to know whether the person who priced that Korean deal looked at the Treasury curve first. Probably they did, and probably they thought the window would stay open a few more weeks.
